questions.q: Why is a circuit validation failure fundamentally different from a device-offline failure, in terms of how orchestration code should respond?
options: A validation failure is a classical bug in the submission code that will fail identically on retry, while a device-offline failure is often transient and can succeed by retrying against a different device
Both should always be retried against the same device with no changes
There is no meaningful difference; both should be treated with the same generic retry logic
A validation failure always costs more money than a device-offline failure
questions.explain: Retrying an invalid circuit against the same (or any) device will fail the same way every time, since the circuit itself violates device constraints. Device-offline failures are often resolved by retrying against an alternate device instead.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, a job fails twice (modes 2/3) before succeeding on attempt 3, on IonQ Aria pricing ($0.30/task + $0.03/shot, 1,000 shots/task). What is the wasted spend from the two failed attempts?
options: $30.30, since only the first failure counts
$90.90, counting all three attempts including the successful one
$60.60, since each failed attempt costs $30.30 (0.30 + 1000x0.03) and there were two of them
$0, since failed jobs are never billed by any provider
questions.explain: Each failed attempt still incurs the per-task fee plus the per-shot fee for shots executed before failure: $0.30 + 1,000x$0.03 = $30.30 per attempt, so two failed attempts waste $60.60.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that error handling can't be one generic try/except: retry block for all failure modes?
options: Quantum cloud providers forbid the use of try/except blocks in client code
All failure modes should always be retried the same number of times regardless of type
Generic retry blocks are technically impossible to write in any language used for quantum orchestration

The correct response genuinely differs by failure mode -- retrying a circuit validation failure (a code bug) wastes retries, while giving up immediately on a transient queue timeout gives up too early on something likely to succeed on retry
questions.explain: The decision table shows retryability genuinely differs by failure type: validation failures are never retryable (same bug fails identically every time), while queue timeouts and transient network errors usually are. A single undifferentiated retry policy mishandles at least one of these cases.

questions.q: When one of 17 parameter-shift circuit evaluations fails within a single optimization iteration, what does the lesson say orchestration code should NOT do?
options: Silently treat the failed evaluation as a zero or drop it without flagging the iteration, feeding an effectively-incomplete gradient into the optimizer as if nothing happened
Mark the failed evaluation explicitly so the issue is visible
Decide whether to retry the failed evaluation based on the failure-mode decision table
Flag the iteration's result as degraded if the failure can't be recovered within budget
questions.explain: Silently dropping or zeroing a failed evaluation corrupts the gradient estimate without anyone noticing. The lesson recommends explicit failure marking, a retry decision per failure mode, and flagging the iteration as degraded if unrecoverable -- not silent substitution.

questions.q: Why can a partial shot completion sometimes be treated as usable rather than requiring a full retry?
options: If enough shots completed to produce an acceptable standard error for the use case, the partial result may still be statistically usable, rather than wasting a full retry
Partial shot completions are never billed, so there's no cost reason to use them
A partial result is always more accurate than a full result
Partial results are always discarded regardless of how many shots completed
questions.explain: Since standard error scales with shot count (1/sqrt(shots), from the post-processing lesson), a partial result with enough shots may already meet the required precision -- making a full retry unnecessary waste, as the decision table notes with 'depends.'
